    84  /**
    85   * SECTION:date-time
    86   * @title: GDateTime
    87   * @short_description: a structure representing Date and Time
    88   * @see_also: #GTimeZone
    89   *
    90   * #GDateTime is a structure that combines a Gregorian date and time
    91   * into a single structure.  It provides many conversion and methods to
    92   * manipulate dates and times.  Time precision is provided down to
    93   * microseconds and the time can range (proleptically) from 0001-01-01
    94   * 00:00:00 to 9999-12-31 23:59:59.999999.  #GDateTime follows POSIX
    95   * time in the sense that it is oblivious to leap seconds.
    96   *
    97   * #GDateTime is an immutable object; once it has been created it cannot
    98   * be modified further.  All modifiers will create a new #GDateTime.
    99   * Nearly all such functions can fail due to the date or time going out
   100   * of range, in which case %NULL will be returned.
   101   *
   102   * #GDateTime is reference counted: the reference count is increased by calling
   103   * g_date_time_ref() and decreased by calling g_date_time_unref(). When the
   104   * reference count drops to 0, the resources allocated by the #GDateTime
   105   * structure are released.
   106   *
   107   * Many parts of the API may produce non-obvious results.  As an
   108   * example, adding two months to January 31st will yield March 31st
   109   * whereas adding one month and then one month again will yield either
   110   * March 28th or March 29th.  Also note that adding 24 hours is not
   111   * always the same as adding one day (since days containing daylight
   112   * savings time transitions are either 23 or 25 hours in length).
   113   *
   114   * #GDateTime is available since GLib 2.26.
   115   */

   117  struct _GDateTime
   118  {
   119    /* Microsecond timekeeping within Day */
   120    guint64 usec;
   121
   122    /* TimeZone information */
   123    GTimeZone *tz;
   124    gint interval;
   125
   126    /* 1 is 0001-01-01 in Proleptic Gregorian */
   127    gint32 days;
   128
   129    gint ref_count;  /* (atomic) */
   130  };

   132  /* Time conversion {{{1 */

   135  #define INSTANT_TO_UNIX(instant) \

   139  #define UNIX_TO_INSTANT(unix) \

  1530   *
  1531   * Creates a new #GDateTime corresponding to the given date and time in
  1532   * the time zone @tz.
  1533   *
  1534   * The @year must be between 1 and 9999, @month between 1 and 12 and @day
  1535   * between 1 and 28, 29, 30 or 31 depending on the month and the year.
  1536   *
  1537   * @hour must be between 0 and 23 and @minute must be between 0 and 59.
  1538   *
  1539   * @seconds must be at least 0.0 and must be strictly less than 60.0.
  1540   * It will be rounded down to the nearest microsecond.
  1541   *
  1542   * If the given time is not representable in the given time zone (for
  1543   * example, 02:30 on March 14th 2010 in Toronto, due to daylight savings
  1544   * time) then the time will be rounded up to the nearest existing time
  1545   * (in this case, 03:00).  If this matters to you then you should verify
  1546   * the return value for containing the same as the numbers you gave.
  1547   *
  1548   * In the case that the given time is ambiguous in the given time zone
  1549   * (for example, 01:30 on November 7th 2010 in Toronto, due to daylight
  1550   * savings time) then the time falling within standard (ie:
  1551   * non-daylight) time is taken.
  1552   *
  1553   * It not considered a programmer error for the values to this function
  1554   * to be out of range, but in the case that they are, the function will
  1555   * return %NULL.
  1556   *
  1557   * You should release the return value by calling g_date_time_unref()
  1558   * when you are done with it.
  1559   *
  1560   * Returns: (transfer full) (nullable): a new #GDateTime, or %NULL
  1561   *
  1562   * Since: 2.26
  1563   **/
  1564  GDateTime *
  1565  g_date_time_new (GTimeZone *tz,
  1566                   gint       year,
  1567                   gint       month,
  1568                   gint       day,
  1569                   gint       hour,
  1570                   gint       minute,
  1571                   gdouble    seconds)
  1572  {
  1573    GDateTime *datetime;
  1574    gint64 full_time;
  1575    /* keep these variables as volatile. We do not want them ending up in
  1576     * registers - them doing so may cause us to hit precision problems on i386.
  1577     * See: https://bugzilla.gnome.org/show_bug.cgi?id=792410 */
  1578    volatile gint64 usec;
  1579    volatile gdouble usecd;
  1580
  1581    g_return_val_if_fail (tz != NULL, NULL);
  1582
  1583    if (year < 1 || year > 9999 ||
  1584        month < 1 || month > 12 ||
  1585        day < 1 || day > days_in_months[GREGORIAN_LEAP (year)][month] ||
  1586        hour < 0 || hour > 23 ||
  1587        minute < 0 || minute > 59 ||
  1588        seconds < 0.0 || seconds >= 60.0)
  1589      return NULL;
  1590
  1591    datetime = g_date_time_alloc (tz);
  1592    datetime->days = ymd_to_days (year, month, day);
  1593    datetime->usec = (hour   * USEC_PER_HOUR)
  1594                   + (minute * USEC_PER_MINUTE)
  1595                   + (gint64) (seconds * USEC_PER_SECOND);
  1596
  1597    full_time = SEC_PER_DAY *
  1598                  (ymd_to_days (year, month, day) - UNIX_EPOCH_START) +
  1599                SECS_PER_HOUR * hour +
  1600                SECS_PER_MINUTE * minute +
  1601                (int) seconds;
  1602
  1603    datetime->interval = g_time_zone_adjust_time (datetime->tz,
  1604                                                  G_TIME_TYPE_STANDARD,
  1605                                                  &full_time);
  1606
  1607    /* This is the correct way to convert a scaled FP value to integer.
  1608     * If this surprises you, please observe that (int)(1.000001 * 1e6)
  1609     * is 1000000.  This is not a problem with precision, it's just how
  1610     * FP numbers work.
  1611     * See https://bugzilla.gnome.org/show_bug.cgi?id=697715. */
  1612    usec = seconds * USEC_PER_SECOND;
  1613    usecd = (usec + 1) * 1e-6;
  1614    if (usecd <= seconds) {
  1615      usec++;
  1616    }
  1617
  1618    full_time += UNIX_EPOCH_START * SEC_PER_DAY;
  1619    datetime->days = full_time / SEC_PER_DAY;
  1620    datetime->usec = (full_time % SEC_PER_DAY) * USEC_PER_SECOND;
  1620    datetime->usec = (full_time % SEC_PER_DAY) * USEC_PER_SECOND;
  1621    datetime->usec += usec % USEC_PER_SECOND;
  1622
  1623    return datetime;
  1624  }

  1685                       gint    day,

  2484  /**
  2485   * g_date_time_get_second:
  2486   * @datetime: a #GDateTime
  2487   *
  2488   * Retrieves the second of the minute represented by @datetime
  2489   *

  2491   *
  2492   * Since: 2.26
  2493   */
  2494  gint
  2495  g_date_time_get_second (GDateTime *datetime)
  2496  {
  2497    g_return_val_if_fail (datetime != NULL, 0);
  2498
  2499    return (datetime->usec % USEC_PER_MINUTE) / USEC_PER_SECOND;

  2504   * @datetime: a #GDateTime

  2513  g_date_time_get_microsecond (GDateTime *datetime)
  2514  {
  2515    g_return_val_if_fail (datetime != NULL, 0);
  2516
  2517    return (datetime->usec % USEC_PER_SECOND);
  2518  }

  2520  /**
  2521   * g_date_time_get_seconds:
  2522   * @datetime: a #GDateTime
  2523   *
  2524   * Retrieves the number of seconds since the start of the last minute,
  2525   * including the fractional part.
  2526   *
  2527   * Returns: the number of seconds
  2528   *
  2529   * Since: 2.26
  2530   **/
  2531  gdouble
  2532  g_date_time_get_seconds (GDateTime *datetime)
  2533  {
  2534    g_return_val_if_fail (datetime != NULL, 0);
  2535
  2536    return (datetime->usec % USEC_PER_MINUTE) / 1000000.0;
  2537  }

  2540  /**
  2541   * g_date_time_to_unix:
  2542   * @datetime: a #GDateTime
  2543   *
  2544   * Gives the Unix time corresponding to @datetime, rounding down to the
  2545   * nearest second.
  2546   *
  2547   * Unix time is the number of seconds that have elapsed since 1970-01-01
  2548   * 00:00:00 UTC, regardless of the time zone associated with @datetime.
  2549   *
  2550   * Returns: the Unix time corresponding to @datetime
  2551   *
  2552   * Since: 2.26
  2553   **/
  2554  gint64
  2555  g_date_time_to_unix (GDateTime *datetime)
  2556  {
  2557    g_return_val_if_fail (datetime != NULL, 0);

  2563   * g_date_time_to_timeval:
  2564   * @datetime: a #GDateTime
  2565   * @tv: a #GTimeVal to modify
  2566   *
  2567   * Stores the instant in time that @datetime represents into @tv.
  2568   *
  2569   * The time contained in a #GTimeVal is always stored in the form of
  2570   * seconds elapsed since 1970-01-01 00:00:00 UTC, regardless of the time
  2571   * zone associated with @datetime.
  2572   *
  2573   * On systems where 'long' is 32bit (ie: all 32bit systems and all
  2574   * Windows systems), a #GTimeVal is incapable of storing the entire
  2575   * range of values that #GDateTime is capable of expressing.  On those
  2576   * systems, this function returns %FALSE to indicate that the time is
  2577   * out of range.
  2578   *
  2579   * On systems where 'long' is 64bit, this function never fails.
  2580   *
  2581   * Returns: %TRUE if successful, else %FALSE
  2582   *
  2583   * Since: 2.26
  2584   * Deprecated: 2.62: #GTimeVal is not year-2038-safe. Use
  2585   *    g_date_time_to_unix() instead.
  2586   **/
